title: How much this costs and how not to get a nasty surprise
promise: You'll be able to say, with a number in dollars, how much your way of working with AI costs you per month. And you'll have a cap in place that actually stops things if something runs away.
why: Marta runs a small accounting firm in Valencia. She wanted an assistant that read her clients' emails and pulled out a summary. She asked ChatGPT for help. At some point, ChatGPT itself told her she needed an API key and a card. An API key is like a password that lets a program use the AI on its own, billed to your card. Marta pasted the key and left the process running on a Friday afternoon. On Monday she had $450 in charges. The program had gotten stuck in a loop, rereading the same emails all night. What hurt wasn't the money: it was having no idea that was even possible. With two checkboxes changed before she started, the maximum charge would have been $10.

theory.title: Two ways to pay, and only one has a brake
theory.text: There are two ways to pay for AI, and confusing them is exactly what causes the scares. The first is subscription: you pay a fixed amount a month and use the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app. When you hit the message limit, the app tells you to wait a while. It doesn't charge you a single extra cent. The second is pay-per-use, and it goes through the API. The API is the side door through which a program talks to the AI, no app, no text box. There you pay for every chunk of text that goes in and every chunk that comes out. And by default there's no ceiling. If you're typing into ChatGPT's, Claude's, or Gemini's text box, you're always in the first case. There it's materially impossible to get a surprise bill. The scare shows up the day someone, or the AI itself, tells you "create an API key and paste it here." And you paste it without having set a cap first. You'll only want the API the day your website or assistant needs to talk to the AI without you there. For example, a chat that handles your customers at three in the morning. As long as it's you writing and you reading, the subscription is all you need.
theory.analogy: The subscription is the phone's flat-rate plan: talk as much as you want, you pay the same at month's end. The API is roaming from fifteen years ago: every minute counts, nobody warns you, and you find out when the bill arrives.
theory.example: Marta didn't need the API to summarize her emails in the morning. She could paste them into Claude and read the summary, within her $25 subscription. She'd only need it if she wanted the summary to appear on its own at 8:00, with nobody at the keyboard. That distinction, "with or without me there," is what decides whether you pay a fixed $25 or an unknown amount.

theory.title: The token, and the snowball effect
theory.text: The AI doesn't count words, it counts tokens (chunks of a word, roughly four letters each). As a practical reference: 1,000 tokens is about 750 words. A million tokens is about 750,000 words, which is nine novels. What goes in and what comes out are billed separately, and output costs about five times more than input. Here's the part almost nobody tells you, and it's the one that stings. Every time you write a new message in a conversation, the app sends the entire conversation again from the start. It does this because the AI has no memory and has to be reminded of everything each time. Your message number 1 sends 700 tokens. Your message number 40, in that same conversation, sends 60,000, because it drags along the previous 39. That's why a long chat doesn't cost forty times the first question: it costs vastly more. And that's why opening a new conversation when you switch topics is the single most effective savings trick there is. On a subscription you don't pay this in dollars, you pay it in messages used up. That's why you run out of quota faster once you've been three hours in the same thread.
theory.analogy: Imagine picking a conversation back up with someone. Before you can say your new sentence, you have to recap everything you've talked about in the last two hours. At the start it's ten seconds. By hour three, it's twenty minutes of recap just to say one sentence.
theory.example: A 40-message session building a website, dragging the history along, adds up to around 1.2 million input tokens. With Claude Sonnet via API (about $3 per million input tokens), that one conversation alone costs you $3.60. Thirty sessions like that in a month is over $100. Those same thirty sessions inside the Claude Pro app cost $25 total, flat rate.

theory.title: The real numbers, in dollars
theory.text: These figures are from August 2026 and shift every few months. Treat them as an order of magnitude and check the exact number on the pricing page before paying. The entry-level plans all sit in the same range. ChatGPT Plus costs about $20 a month, Claude Pro about $20, and Google AI Pro $19.99. The big plans are a different league. ChatGPT Pro runs around $200 a month. Claude Max ranges from about $100 to about $200 depending on how much usage you want. All of them have a free version that's genuinely good enough to try, with fewer messages a day and weaker models once you push it. On pay-per-use, prices are given per million tokens and vary a lot by model. A large model like Claude Opus is around $15 per million input tokens and $75 output. A mid-tier one, like Claude Sonnet or GPT-4o, around $3 and $15. A small one, like GPT-4o mini or Gemini Flash, around $0.15 and $0.60. Between the large and the small there's a hundredfold difference. And for half of all tasks, the small one does exactly the same job. The rule that works: if you're the one typing, subscription; if a program is writing on its own, pay-per-use with a cap set.
theory.example: For Marta's assistant, summarizing 200 emails a month is about 300,000 input tokens and 60,000 output tokens. With GPT-4o mini: $0.05 input and $0.04 output, so 9 cents a month. With Claude Opus, the same job costs $9.30. A hundred times more expensive to summarize an email, a task the cheapest model handles just fine.

theory.title: The three scares that actually happen
theory.text: The first is auto-recharge. When you put a card into a pay-per-use platform, a checkbox comes pre-enabled. That checkbox charges you another $10 or $20 the moment your balance drops below a certain point. And again, and again. A looping program can trigger that recharge forty times in one night with nobody stopping it. That's exactly what happened to Marta. The second is a leaked key. If you paste your API key somewhere public, bots scan for it within minutes. They use it to burn through your balance. A public place is, for example, an open GitHub repository or a forum post. Publishing a key is irreversible: you can't unpublish it. You can only go into the console, delete it, and create another, and it has to happen the same day. The third is the agent that starts working on its own, the modern version of the loop. You give the AI permission to run things and to retry when they fail, something fails in a loop, and it retries eight thousand times. All three have the same antidote, and it isn't watching closely: it's making sure there's no money available to spend.
theory.example: Imagine that on a Saturday you accidentally publish an OpenAI key in a public GitHub repository. By Monday it could rack up hundreds of dollars in usage. If that account has $20 of prepaid credit and auto-recharge turned off, the maximum damage is $20. That's the whole difference.

theory.title: A warning is not a cap
theory.text: This is the confusion that costs the most, so read it twice. There are two different things that look a lot alike: the alert and the hard limit. The alert emails you saying "you've spent $50" and stops absolutely nothing. If you're asleep, the email arrives and the spending keeps going. The hard limit cuts off the service and returns an error, and that actually ends it. Google Cloud's budget alerts, for example, only warn: they cut off nothing, and a lot of people believe otherwise until it happens to them. The cap that really works is prepaid credit with auto-recharge turned off. I'd recommend it even if you have other caps set. You put in $20 and, when it's gone, it's gone: there's nowhere else to pull more from. On top of that, if your bank allows it, set up a virtual card with a $25 monthly limit. That's the second lock, and it doesn't depend on the platform behaving well. They're two independent locks, and neither needs you watching.
theory.analogy: A warning is the gas light turning on. A hard cap is the tank only holding five liters, period. With the light you can keep driving for three hours ignoring it; with five liters, you can't.
theory.example: A concrete setup to sleep soundly with the OpenAI API: $20 prepaid credit, auto-recharge off, monthly limit $15, and email alert at $10. If something goes haywire, the most you can lose is $20. And you find out when the program starts erroring, not when the bill arrives.

theory.title: What it costs to keep your idea alive on the internet
theory.text: AI is only one of the bills, and it's usually not even the sneakiest one. If your project ends up as a website or a store, three more expenses show up. Hosting is someone else's computer where your site lives so people can visit it. It's free on Vercel or Netlify while it's just you and a few friends. It jumps to about $20 a month once you grow. The domain (the name people type, like myshop.com) costs between $5 and $15 a year. It's paid once a year and is one of the few honest expenses out there. The database is the storage where orders, customers, and content get saved. It has a free plan on Supabase or Neon, and rises to about $25 a month once you fill it up. All these services have the same trap as the API. The free plan doesn't cut you off when you go over: it starts billing you the overage. And that overage is measured in things you don't control, like how many people visit your site. Before connecting a card to any of them, check their settings for an option to "pause the project instead of charging me." Several have it, and almost nobody turns it on.
theory.example: A real project from someone starting out, with traffic from friends: domain $12 a year, hosting on Vercel free, database on Supabase free, Claude Pro subscription $20 a month. Total: about $21 a month, rounding. And of that $21, twenty is the subscription you were already paying to work.

tasks.title: Write down what you're already paying for AI
tasks.where: In your browser, on the site of each AI you use: chatgpt.com, claude.ai, gemini.google.com
tasks.action: Log into each with your account. Find your initial or your photo at bottom left or top right, click it, and go to "Settings." Inside, look for the section that says "Subscription," "Plan," or "Billing." Write down three things per service, on paper or in a note: which plan you have, how much you pay a month, and what day it renews. If it says "Free," write that too: it's just as valid information.
tasks.expect: A list of three or four lines like: "Claude — Pro — $20/mo — renews on the 14th." With that you now know your fixed AI spend, a number most people can't state off the top of their head.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the menu, type into that same AI's text box: "Where do I see what plan I'm on and how much I pay? Give me the exact menu path." And if you see charges from a service you don't remember signing up for, don't cancel it in a hurry yet. Note it down, keep going with the lesson, and look at it calmly at the end.

tasks.title: Check whether your pay-per-use door is open
tasks.where: In your browser, at platform.openai.com and console.anthropic.com
tasks.action: These two addresses are the pay-per-use consoles, different from the regular chat apps. Log in with the same account you use to chat. On OpenAI go to "Settings" then "Billing"; on Anthropic, "Settings" then "Billing" or "Plans." Check two things: whether there's a card saved and whether there's a balance or usage. If it tells you there's no billing account, balance is $0, and no card, great. You have no open doors and can skip the next two tasks.
tasks.expect: One of two things will happen. Either you see a message like "no payment method" and zero balance, meaning you're safe. Or you see a saved card and a balance, in which case you need to do the next two tasks today.
tasks.stuck: If you can't get in because it asks you to create an organization or verify a phone number, stop there and don't do it. You don't need that account for anything in this course yet. Not having one is the safest state there is.

tasks.title: Turn off auto-recharge
tasks.where: At platform.openai.com, Settings → Billing section (and the equivalent at console.anthropic.com)
tasks.action: Do this only if in the previous task you saw a saved card. Inside "Billing" look for a section called "Auto recharge" or "Automatic recharge." It's usually on by default and says something like "when balance drops below $5, recharge $10." Turn that switch off and save. Warning: money already spent doesn't come back. This only protects you going forward, which is why you do it now, not after something happens.
tasks.expect: The switch grayed out or off, and text saying the balance won't recharge on its own. From here on, once the credit runs out, programs will error out instead of continuing to charge you. And that's exactly what you want.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find that option, just remove the saved card with "Remove payment method" and add credit by hand when you need it. It's more inconvenient and it's safer. If the platform won't let you remove the card, skip to the virtual card task: that fixes it from your bank's side, without depending on them.

tasks.title: Set a monthly spending cap and an alert
tasks.where: At platform.openai.com, Settings → Limits (or Budgets) section
tasks.action: Look in the left sidebar for an entry called "Limits," "Usage limits," or "Budgets." You'll see two different checkboxes, and they're not the same thing. One is the alert, usually called "notification threshold" or "soft limit." The other is the cutoff, called "hard limit" or "monthly budget." Set the alert at $10 and the cutoff at $15. Save with the "Save" button. On Anthropic's console the equivalent lives under "Billing" or the workspace settings, look for "spend limit."
tasks.expect: Both numbers saved and visible when you reload the page. When you hit $10 you'll get an email. Once you hit $15, requests will start failing with a quota error, which is the sign the brake is working.
tasks.stuck: If it only lets you set the alert and not the cutoff, no problem: your real cap is going to be the prepaid credit with auto-recharge off, which you've already done. An alert only warns, so don't count it as protection.

tasks.title: Calculate the cost of your idea before building anything
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app, in the usual text box
tasks.action: Open a new conversation and paste the prompt below, replacing what's in brackets with your real idea. When it gives you the table, don't just accept it. Take the two or three biggest numbers and look them up yourself on each service's pricing page. Prices change and the AI is pulling from memory.
tasks.prompt:
I want to build this: [describe your idea in three sentences: what it does, who it's for, and roughly how many people a month you think will use it]. I don't know how to code and I'm going to work with you from this app. Before starting I want to know what it's actually going to cost me, in real dollars, per month.

Give me a table with these columns: item, free option, paid option, monthly cost in dollars, and exactly what happens if I go over the free tier. Include every relevant item: the AI subscription I already pay for, website hosting, the domain, the database, sending emails, the payment gateway, and pay-per-use AI if my project ever needs to call the AI on its own without me present.

For each line tell me whether the cost is fixed or could spike. For the ones that could spike, give me the realistic worst case with a specific number and how to set a cap, with the name of the menu where it's set.

Don't give me vague ranges like "it depends": give me a single figure, tell me what date you think it's from, and tell me to double-check it myself.

End with two sentences: which version of my idea costs $0 a month, and exactly what I lose by choosing that version.
tasks.expect: A table with concrete dollar figures and, at the end, a free version of your idea. The surprise is usually a pleasant one: what you had in mind costs between $0 and $25 a month, not $300.
tasks.stuck: If it answers with generalities and huge ranges, reply: "You wandered off. Pick the most common option for someone starting out, give me one figure per line, and if you're missing something, assume it and tell me what you assumed."

tasks.title: Decide with numbers whether upgrading your plan pays off
tasks.where: In the AI app you use daily
tasks.action: This question will come up the moment you start working seriously: you run out of messages mid-afternoon and the app offers you the plan above. Before paying $100 more a month on impulse, paste this prompt in a new conversation. And answer honestly whatever it asks you.
tasks.prompt:
I'm on the [plan name] plan and pay [X] $ a month. I run out of messages about [N] times a week, and it usually happens when I'm doing [describe the specific task]. The plan above costs [Z] $ a month.

Help me decide with numbers, not opinions. Do it in this order:

1. Before calculating anything, ask me how many hours a week I lose waiting for the limit to reset and how much an hour of my time is worth. Wait for my answer.
2. With that data, compare the cost of waiting against the price difference between the two plans, and tell me above how many lost hours it becomes worth upgrading.
3. Give me three concrete ways to use less quota doing the same work, applied to the task I described, not generic tips.
4. Tell me in what case I should NOT upgrade.

If your conclusion is that I shouldn't upgrade, tell me clearly even if it looks like I want to.
tasks.expect: A concrete threshold like "it's worth upgrading if you lose more than 2.5 hours a week." Often the right answer is not to upgrade and to open new conversations more often instead, which is free.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you the whole comparison without asking anything, tell it: "You skipped step 1. Ask me the two questions and wait for my answer before calculating."

tasks.title: Get yourself a virtual card with a limit
tasks.where: In your banking app: Revolut, N26, Chime, and most banks offer this
tasks.action: Look in your banking app for "virtual card," "disposable card," or "subscription card." Create a new one and set a monthly spending limit of $25, or whatever you decided in the calculation task. Use that card, and only that card, for anything related to AI, hosting, and databases. Your main card doesn't go anywhere near these sites.
tasks.expect: A new card in your app with a visible monthly limit. From here on, the charge gets declined once it hits the limit you set. It doesn't matter if the platform's own cap fails, if your key leaks, or if there's a loop.
tasks.stuck: If your bank doesn't offer virtual cards with a limit, there's an alternative that works just as well. Use a secondary bank account with $30 in it and its linked card. What can't happen is the card you use having all your savings behind it.

tasks.title: Translate your bill with the AI
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT or Claude app, with the spending breakdown open in another tab
tasks.action: Do this once now, and then once a month. Go into the "Usage" section of whichever platform you're paying for. Take a screenshot or copy the breakdown's text. Paste it to the AI with this prompt. Before pasting anything, black out or remove any card number or key that shows up: it's not needed for the analysis.
tasks.prompt:
I'm going to paste my [OpenAI / Anthropic / Vercel / Supabase] account's spending breakdown for this month. Translate it into plain, everyday language, as if you were explaining it to someone who's never coded.

Tell me, in this order:
1. How much I've spent in total, in dollars, and whether that's trending higher or lower than last month.
2. Which three line items eat up most of the money and what they actually are, in normal words.
3. If you see any charge that doesn't fit with the idea that I'm the only one using this, by hand, during office hours.
4. Three concrete changes that would cut next month's bill in half, ordered from biggest to smallest saving.
5. Whether you spot any sign that something might be running on its own without me knowing: overnight usage, repeated spikes, identical requests back to back.

If anything in the breakdown is unclear or you're missing context, ask me instead of assuming.

Here's the breakdown:
[paste here]
tasks.expect: A summary in dollars with the three biggest expense lines and, above all, a clear answer to point 5. Spotting usage at 4 in the morning is the fastest way to catch a loop before it gets expensive.
tasks.stuck: If the screenshot comes out unreadable or the text pastes in a jumble, ask instead: "Walk me through exporting the breakdown to CSV from this screen." And if it says it can't read the image, copy and paste the text instead of the screenshot.

tasks.title: Write your cost sheet and set yourself a reminder
tasks.where: In a note on your phone or a document, and on your calendar
tasks.action: Gather what you found today into a single note. Write down four things: the plans you pay for, with their price and renewal date; whether you have pay-per-use open or not; what caps you've set; and which card you pay with. Four or five lines is enough. Then open your calendar and create a recurring monthly 10-minute event called "Review AI spending," on the 1st. In those 10 minutes you do only one thing: the previous task, pasting your bill to the AI.
tasks.prompt:
Help me write my cost sheet: a short note I want to be able to glance at six months from now and understand without remembering anything.

Here's what I gathered today:
- AI subscriptions I pay for: [paste what you wrote down: service, plan, monthly price, renewal date]
- Do I have pay-per-use open?: [yes or no, and on which platforms]
- Caps I've set: [prepaid credit you added, monthly limit, alert, virtual card and its limit]
- Other project services: [domain, hosting, database, and what you pay for each]

Give me a note of ten lines at most, in plain text with no flourishes, that includes: the total fixed amount I pay per month in dollars, the worst realistic monthly case if everything spiked at once, what day of the month my first charge hits, and one final line saying what's the first thing to check if some month I get a charge I wasn't expecting.

If the worst case can't be calculated with the data I gave you because I'm missing a cap I haven't set, don't make up the number: tell me exactly which cap is missing and where to set it.
tasks.expect: A note you can show anyone and a recurring monthly event. If someone asks how much your project costs, you answer with a figure in three seconds.
tasks.stuck: If you can't be bothered to write it, tell the AI out loud and ask: "With what I just told you, write me a five-line cost sheet I can paste into a note." And if the 1st is a bad day, put it on the day your most expensive subscription renews: that way you review it right before you get charged.

matters: Turning off auto-recharge before putting your card into any pay-per-use platform. It's a checkbox that comes enabled by default. It's the exact mechanism by which a $2 glitch turns into $400. Without it, your maximum spend is whatever balance you have. With it, there's no maximum.

Knowing how to tell an alert apart from a cap. Almost everyone who gets a nasty surprise had an alert set and thought they had a brake. The email arrived at 3am and the spending kept running until 9. If it only lets you set an alert, your real brake needs to be prepaid credit or a virtual card.

Never pasting an API key somewhere public: an open GitHub repo, a forum, a screenshot on Twitter. There are bots that find them in minutes. Publishing it is irreversible. The only fix is going into the console, deleting that key, and creating another one, and it has to happen the same day.

Being clear that almost everything you want to do fits inside the $20 subscription you already pay for. Ignore that and you end up building things via the API that never needed it, with an open-ended bill. All to do exactly the same thing you were already doing by typing into the text box.
ignore: Optimizing tokens down to the letter: shortening prompts, counting characters, hunting for shorter words. The savings are pennies and the time you lose is worth more. The only thing that actually moves the needle is opening a new conversation when you switch topics, and that's free and takes one second.

Prompt caching, batch requests, and volume discounts. Prompt caching is the AI reusing text you already sent it before. Batch requests are sending it many at once and waiting for the response. All three cut pay-per-use costs a lot, but they start mattering when you're spending hundreds of dollars a month. You'll know when you get there because you'll see it on the bill, and that'll be the moment.

Comparing the thirty models out there and their pricing tables. There are only three categories: large and expensive, mid-tier, and small and cheap. Between the extremes there's about a hundredfold difference. Knowing that gets you 95% of the decisions right.
canDo: Estimate how many tokens a text you paste will use and translate it into dollars given the model's price. If you give it a real sample of your data, the estimate comes out fairly accurate.
Translate a bill or usage breakdown into plain language. It also flags which three line items eat up the money. And it catches odd patterns, like overnight usage or repeated requests.

Suggest a cheaper version of what you want to build. It tells you which smaller model handles the same task and which part can be done without AI at all. And it tells you what the $0-a-month version of your idea looks like.
Walk you step by step through the menus to set caps, turn off recharges, or export usage. For that, tell it which platform you're on and paste what's on your screen.
cantDo: It can't see your account or know how much you've spent right now. If it gives you a usage figure without you having pasted it, it's making that up.
It can't set the caps for you. Configuring the limit, turning off recharge, and creating the virtual card are things you have to do yourself with your own mouse, and they take ten minutes.

It gets current prices wrong, and does so with a lot of confidence. It's pulling from what it learned months ago and prices move. Whatever two or three figures actually matter to you, check them on the pricing page.
It doesn't warn you while you're spending. There's no moment where the AI tells you "hey, this conversation is already at $4." That alert has to come from the caps you set, never from it.
words: Token
The small chunk the AI splits text into to count it, roughly four letters. You pay per chunk, not per word: a thousand chunks is about seven hundred fifty words.
API
The side door through which a program talks to the AI. No app, no text box, no person in front of it. You pay for what you use, not a flat fee.
Pay-per-use
Paying for every bit consumed, like water or electricity. There's no maximum amount unless you set one by hand.
Auto-recharge
A checkbox that means, once your balance runs out, another chunk gets charged to your card automatically, and again, and again. It usually comes pre-enabled and is the usual cause of huge charges.
Prepaid credit
Money you put in ahead of time that gets spent down. When it hits zero, it stops working, period. It's the most reliable brake because it doesn't depend on anyone warning you.
Hard limit
An amount that, once reached, actually cuts off the service and stops things from working. Different from an alert, which just sends an email and stops nothing.
Context window
Everything the AI is looking at right now to answer you, which includes the entire conversation from the start. The longer the chat, the bigger it gets, and the more each new message costs.
Hosting
Another company's computer where your site lives, running all day, so anyone can visit even with your own computer off.
Domain
The name people type to reach your site, like myshop.com. It's rented by the year, not bought forever.
Billable overage
What you get charged when you go over what your plan includes. The trap is that you don't get cut off when you hit the limit: they let you keep going and just keep tallying it.
next: With your spending bounded and your caps set, you move on to building the first version of your idea knowing the worst that can happen costs you $20.
